description:
Nvidia has "RTX" plastered on the names of their graphics cards yet they do not equip most of their 'lower-tier' GPUs with enough VRAM to take advantage of it. Enter AMD with the RX 9060 XT 16GB- ignoring the 8GB version of the card for the time, the 16GB one can actually hold up super well in RTX lmao. So, let's take a look.

RX 9060 XT 16GB (Asus Prime OC, $350- the one I have): https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1900328-REG/asus_prime_rx9060xt_o16g_radeon_rx_9060_xt.html

comments.text:
I mean honestly, if they just did the right thing and advertised it as what it actually is - a 50-50ti series card and put the appropriate price under it, then nobody would bat an eye. This level of performance is quite good coming from a 50 series card, but everything else about it is just abysmal. 
Like, would it cost them that much? To just get the appreciation and respect back?

comments.text:
One aspect that also has to be talked about, are hardware features that are required for some non-gaming scenarios: Stable Diffusion, Blender etc. 
In those scenarios you won't have a choice but to buy an Nvidia card. That's unfortunate, because if I only played games on my PC, I would have bought another AMD gpu. So I upgraded to a used RTX 3070 to also be able to benefit in non-gaming scenarios. That being said, I am able to play Cyberpunk 2077 (with DLSS Quality and RT) with 60FPS most of the time. DLSS Quality has no notable visual impact, so I do not have problems using it. Yes, it may drop down to like 40-ish fps in some scenes, but it's still playble with low latency features and FreeSync enabled. Apart from that I put everything to highest settings (with crowd density being the only exception). Got the 3070 for 240€ used and it definitely is a lot better than my old RX 5700. I also probably can expect more fps once I can replace my 550W psu. I also upgraded to a Ryzen 7 5800X (because my old R5 3600 certainly is a bottleneck) and put it in ECO mode to have less strain on my PSU, which will be replaced with a 750W PSU in a few days. I'm more curious about the cpu bound game performance of these cards. The 9000 series doesn't have the minimum core clock rate settings anymore and minecraft at minimum settings is so light of a load on the gpu (9070xt) that it doesn't change from what it idles at and bc of that it got me around 4-9fps. If I upscale to 4k (from 1080p) and max everything then I get a 11000% increase in fps but even still it only raised to about 2.1GHz at max. The game clock was 2.45GHz on that card and boost was 2.95GHz, so overclocking wouldn't matter since it can't even reach normal clocks. I wonder just how the clearly severely underpowered 5060 performs on stuff like that, I only have experience with the 9070xt and know that it's garbage unless you only play flagship stuff at max settings.

"100% faster on the 1% lows."
Lows represent how much the graphics card is stuttering—these are the bottom percentile of framerates where dips occur. Wow, I didn’t know that! Thanks. How do people not talk about this more? It’s such an important metric.
What’s shocking is that a lot of sixth-gen games ran at a solid 60 FPS and were much more fun as well. Darkwatch, Manhunt on the Xbox, F-Zero GX, Wario World on the GameCube, Devil May Cry 1–3, Crash Twinsanity on the PS2, etc.—I’ve never seen any stuttering in those games. Ever.
It feels like the quality of programming has dropped significantly. The ones still doing great work are usually developers with experience on older hardware.
Honestly, I still think Silent Hill 3 looks better on the PS2—for that hardware—than Cyberpunk does on the PS5. Back then, hardware was usually pushed to its limits after about three years. With the PS5, it feels like it’s just being abused for convenience, and not pushed to its full potential.
And yeah, good old 2000s PC games were optimized so well. On launch, you could play Mafia with 2–4x SSAA anti-aliasing and still get solid framerates on a GeForce 2. No upscaling, no AI, no frame generation, etc.
What’s frustrating is that I grew up with SSAA, and now TAA is the standard. I already wear strong glasses and the world is blurry enough—I don’t want my games to be blurry and smeared too.
PCSX2 is the savior.

comments.text:
GTX to RTX was meaningless. Because RTX isn't a API. Its only a GPU Moniker. Ray Tracing only works via DX12 or Vulkan API's. So RTX? you're just falling for Nvidia marketing, aka you're not smart.... Even when Nvidia says "we are better at ray tracing than our competitor" memes, that isn't because they invented anything. Microsoft DirectX 12 updates their API, then Nvidia adopts the newest updates to give higher performance. So for example when Nvidia was originally saying "New BVH Traversal Engine" no, they didn't invent anything. That was LITEARLLY part of the DX12 update for that year/timeframe. Nvidia just adopted it as quickly as possible. "Well then why does Nvidia typically beat AMD at Ray Tracing?" because shaders. First breaking down the meme. When a GPU Shader renders an RT workload, technically its an "RT CORE." RT cores in the sense of actual separate cores on the GPU do, not, exist. So that's why when you see a Nvidia 5090 with 170 graphics cores (170 SM's) it also magically has 170 RT cores. The RT core count ALWAYS 100% matches the GPU core count. Why? Because RT cores dont actually exist! Because IF RT cores existed, we could in theory have a high end gpu (for example) that has 170 graphics cores but 340 RT cores.... that will never happen, because all graphics cards are "generic compute devices" which render most things inside "the gpu shader." The microsoft directx12 ray tracing white paper? literally tells you all their "functions" for rendering ray tracing in a video game is pushed through gpu shaders. its all there in the white paper/technical data for everyone to read.... for free. So, back to the question, why is Nvidia typically faster at RT than AMD gpu for gpu. Well the first answer is shaders per core. Here comes the list....

Nvidia 2000 series AKA their first "RTX" GPU's.... 64 shaders per core.
Nvidia 3000 series.... 128 shaders per core
Nvidia 4000 series.... 128 shaders per core
Nvidia 5000 series.... 128 shaders per core
AMD 6000 series.... 64 shaders per core
AMD 7000 series.... 64 shaders per core
AMD 9000 series.... 64 shaders per core

Notice the meme yet? Nvidia went full brute force and doubled their shaders per core after a single generation realizing that 64 shaders per core wasn't enough to handle ray tracing. Granted, back then, they also didn't have parallel processing either. Well, they did, but it was dogshit. It wasn't as good as AMD's asynchronous compute.... the 3000 series kinda improved that, but still wasn't as good as AMD. so the 128 shaders per core really helped in RT workloads. the 4000 series is when Nvidia's asynchronous compute really got better/improved. and the 5000 series is just another brute force product, no real change to architecture just "more cores" as proven by the lack of performance of lower end cards (5060 basically being the same as a 4060 in terms of real world fps, the same meme for 3060 to 4060, no real gains to be seen). And then the retards of the world would go "so then why does the 4090 beat the 3090 if they have the same amount of shaders per core?" because the 3090 only has 82 SM's/Cores while the 4090 had 128 SM's/Cores.... more cores=more shaders. 128x82=10496 while 128x128=16,384.... of course the 4090 was faster. it has more cores AND more shaders. derp.

AMD, could right now, release their next series of GPU's with 128 shaders per core, and probably BEAT Nvidia in ray tracing flat out. Why? Because AMD didn't just bump up to more shaders, they tried to ensure the shaders they had were as efficient as possible. Changing the gpu architecture as a whole to perform better. But they will always be limited by size, which is why GPU's are always adding more cores. Because there is always a limitation in that regards. Intel learned the hardway, that making the same product over and over again without any sweeping changes and only focusing on tweaking and architecture to make it better results in losing ground. And now AMD sells the best CPU's on the market. Sadly if AMD keeps going down the "tweak it and make it better" meme for GPU's, they will fall further behind Nvidia on the high end. Which they basically did as they refused to compete vs Nvidia this generation.... literally a 70 class card only? AMD is only selling 60/70 class cards right now. pathetic. Sure, their 9070xt is basically a 7900xtx.... they should have had FASTER cards for people like me who already have a 7900xtx to buy. why would I buy a 9070xt when my 7900xtx already has the same performance (and honestly in some games, my 7900xtx is faster). I loath this AMD meme of slow cards. I want fast cards. I want next gen performance. Not last gen performance. I paid $1000 for my 7900xtx red devil from microcenter. The 9070xt is the SAME performance for the SAME price.... what happened to offering more performance? That my gripe with AMD. We used to get newer cards for the same price as last gen that were faster. The 6900xt was about $1000 and the 7900xtx was about a $1000 and the 7900xtx is ABSOLUTELY faster than the 6900xt.... for the same price.... now you get the same performance for the same price? shoot me.

I really do think ray tracing is worth it, at least as a technology that hardware and software should pursue.
It can drastically change a scene, and I have taken so many comparison photos of cyberpunk and Alan wake 2 with path tracing on and off, and the differences are very noticeable. (My favourite scenes are ones with complex shaped emissive lights, as it's currently impossible through normal techniques)
The reflections make metals look more like metal, the shadows don't suffer from pixelation or acne/self-shadows, and the global illumination is just on another level, not to mention this doesn't require baking so scenes can be dynamic!!!
Though the performance hit means path tracing is really only achievable on the more expensive cards, and I just don't think they're worth the insane price (I bought one, and it costs waaaay too much)

I am very excited to see it become the norm in the next decade (wish it was sooner, but progress feels very sluggish atm)

The only detail you got wrong is that the GPU cores can't load in more data, the GPU has to rely on the CPU to give it access to the system RAM, which is much slower. So when you run out of VRAM, you don't need to use as many cores to run at the max FPS your GPU can provide, which means that there are a bunch of cores on standby doing nothing. It's basically as if the GPU put an FPS limit on itself.

Problem is DLSS does stuff that make Ray/path tracing run better

And no i am not talking about just upscaling and frame generation

I mean the ray reconstruction part and some other stuff that make RT/PT look better and run better

The upscaling part makes the raw power of the card work less because it renders less resolution and then offloads that to the special hardware tensor cores and uses totally different cores that would otherwise be unused

And that's how you get extra FPS because the raw GPU works less

Now ray/path tracing runs on RT cores
And ray reconstruction makes RT/PT look better and it runs better because the denoising part of the rendering got cut so it does less steps to denoise so it's faster to denoise and still looks better

Same with FSR 4 and soon Redstone thing

comments.text: I part-way blame DLSS/FSR/XeSS for that. Not because upscaling is a bad tech that shouldn't help or anything, no not at all. It's because developers look at the 50-200% extra performance upscaling can yield and say "I'll have that for some extra effects thank you very much". What this tech has allowed is the console approach of game development (graphics maxxing at the cost of render scale) to be applied to PC games. Developers have taken this useful tool that helps people with older cards or restricted budgets, and exploited it to effectively rob people of that performance benefit. And the result is often an uglier game too, because despite the quality of the upscaling, there's simply no replacement for pixel displacement.

RX 9070XT fait 6% de moin que la 7900XTX (pourtant la 7900XTX est bien plus haut de gamme que la 9070XT).
RX9070XT fait 6% de moins que la 4080 .
RX9070XT fait 7% de moins que la 4080Super .
RX9070XT fait 20% de moin que la 5080 (normal la 5080 est bien plus haut de gamme , AMD n'ont pas encore sorti de GPU similaire/voir meilleur pour l'instant) sachant que la 5080 est dans le top 3 mondial . 
RX9070XT fait 39% de moin que la 4090 .
Et pour finir la 9070XT fait 82% de moin que la 5090 32Gb (déjà rien que le bus 512 bits vs 256bit , et 16Gb vs 32 Gb c'est donc logique que la 5090 soit dans le top 1).

Comme je le disais AMD n'ont toujours pas remplacer les 7900XT/XTX/7900GRE donc c'est logique, mais quand même surprenant de voir une carte à 750/850$ ce classer dans le top 8 mondiale . Ce qui prouve que cette année AMD Radeon domine largement NVIDIA car on sait tous que les 5080/5090 seront les moins bonne vente du catalogue NVIDIA les gens iront sur des 5060Ti et 5070Ti pour la plupart . Donc dans la même cours qu'AMD . J'espère vraiment que la 9080XT 32Gb n'est pas une Fake news sinon je serais vraiment déçu même si je sais qu'ils ont déjà sorti une variante PRO de la 9070XT > la Radeon AI PRO R9700 32Gb , qui est juste une 9070XT mais avec 32Gb de VRAM (vous pouvez vérifier elle est bien déjà sortie) , si ils sont capables de sortir des Radeon 8040S/8050S/8060S/R9700 , ils sont bien capable de sortir d'autres variante dans les prochains mois donc c'est à surveiller .
